JOHANNESBURG, South Africa (CNN) -- The atmosphere was tense in Cape Town on Friday after xenophobic violence that has left more than 40 dead in Johannesburg spread to South Africa's largest city. Immigrants from Mozambique line up in Primrose, South Africa, to board buses back home. Clashes overnight resulted in one death and 15 arrests and the evacuations of 420 foreign nationals, a police official in Cape Town said. "Crowds of people went on a rampage, looting and carrying out acts of violence," said Cape Town Police Superintendent Billy Jones. They were charged with public violence and are to appear in court Monday. One foreign national, a Somali, died when he was run over by a vehicle as he tried to escape the angry crowds, Jones said. Twelve people suffered minor injuries. He said Friday was tense but calm, with state and local police stationed throughout the area. Jack Bloom of the opposition party Democratic Alliance told CNN on Friday that government troops were helping police ward off violence in Johannesburg. Aid workers and volunteers were providing tents, food and supplies at the police stations. Bloom estimated that about 2,000 foreigners had sought haven at those locations. It was the first violence in the coastal city since a wave of xenophobia began about two weeks ago in Johannesburg, resulting in at least 42 deaths. The foreign nationals were transported from the city after angry crowds formed at a public meeting seeking to calm tensions, Jones told CNN. They were being housed at community centers and churches. The attacks in South Africa have forced thousands of immigrants to flee, prompting neighboring Mozambique to declare a state of emergency on Friday. Desperate stories of those fleeing violence . The country's Foreign Minister Oldemiro Baloi said the decision was taken after about 10,000 Mozambicans fled from South Africa. CNN's Robyn Curnow reported long lines of people -- including many from Zimbabwe and Mozambique -- waiting for buses in Johannesburg to take them home. Bloom, from Gauteng province, which includes Johannesburg, said the attacks on foreigners who fled to South Africa for a better life has become a "humanitarian crisis." South African President Thabo Mbeki has approved the deployment of the army to help stop the attacks, which have drawn condemnation from South African officials and other African leaders. About 28,000 people have been displaced by the violence, Hangwani Malaudzi, a spokesman for the Ministry of Safety and Security said. And more than 400 have been arrested for crimes ranging from murder, to causing a public disturbance, he said. The country has also seen a disturbing throwback to the 1980s apartheid-era lynching tactic of "necklacing," which was widely used in the townships at the time. Used on suspected informants, the "necklace" is a car tire, filled with petrol, put around the person's neck and set alight. The victims are mainly immigrants and refugees from other parts of Africa, including Zimbabwe, where a devastated economy has sent at least two million people across the border in search of a better life. Some say the attacks stem from a long-standing feeling among locals that the number of immigrants in South Africa results in shortages of jobs and essential needs. Inadequate housing, a lack of running water and electricity, the rising prices of food, and escalating crime -- nearly 20,000 people were slain in South Africa last year -- add to the resentment.  Watch analysis of reasons behind xenophobic attacks » . According to South Africa's latest census, the country has about 45 million people. The South African Department of Human Affairs estimates that more than 4 million people reside in South Africa illegally, but that figure is based on a 10-year-old study and some feel the number of immigrants in South Africa is much higher. Some say that millions have recently fled to South Africa from Zimbabwe because of violence there since the county's stalled election. A presidential run-off between long-time leader President Robert Mugabe and his opposition challenger, Morgan Tsvangirai, is scheduled for June 27 in Zimbabwe -- three months after the initial vote. Zimbabwe also is in the midst of an economic collapse, with nearly 80 percent unemployment.

What began as localized skirmishes in the informal settlements of Johannesburg has spiraled into a full-blown national crisis and regional diplomatic emergency. Over the past two weeks, a wave of deadly xenophobic violence has swept across South Africa, moving from the congested townships of Gauteng province to the coastal communities of Cape Town. The brutal attacks, driven by deep-seated economic frustration and anti-immigrant sentiment, have left over 40 people dead, hundreds injured, and tens of thousands displaced.

The violence erupted in the historic township of Alexandra, just north of Johannesburg, where armed mobs turned on foreign nationals—primarily migrants from neighboring African nations such as Mozambique, Zimbabwe, Malawi, and Somalia. Fueled by false accusations that immigrants were taking scarce jobs, driving up crime rates, and straining public services, the unrest spread rapidly. Gangs wielding clubs, pangas, and petrol bombs targeted foreign-owned businesses, dragged families from their homes, and set light to informal settlements. Within days, similar scenes of chaos played out in Durban and the townships surrounding Cape Town, where plumes of smoke marked the destruction of immigrant neighborhoods.

Security forces utilized tear gas, rubber bullets, and armored vehicles to disperse crowds and enforce curfews in high-risk zones. 

Concurrently, a massive humanitarian emergency response was mobilized. Humanitarian organizations, including the Red Cross, local charities, and faith-based groups, worked frantically alongside state agencies to evacuate targeted foreign nationals from danger zones. Thousands of terrified refugees—carrying little more than the clothes on their backs—were ferried under armed escort to makeshift temporary shelters set up in community halls, police station courtyards, churches, and athletic stadiums.

The border post at Ressano Garcia became a scene of overwhelming congestion as thousands of terrified migrants attempted to flee back to their home countries by any means necessary—on packed buses, in flatbed trucks, and on foot.

The sudden, chaotic influx of thousands of destitute and traumatized citizens forced neighboring Mozambique to officially declare a state of emergency. The violence has not only left a trail of physical destruction and loss of life, but it has also fractured relations between South Africa and its African neighbors, leaving an enduring stain on the nation's post-apartheid identity.

**Johannesburg: The Beating Heart of South Africa**

Nestled on the dusty highveld plateau, **Johannesburg** stands as the powerful economic and cultural engine of **South Africa**. Often referred to by its vibrant nicknames—Jozi, Jo'burg, or *eGoli* (the City of Gold)—this sprawling metropolis is a place of unstoppable energy, profound historical depth, and constant reinvention. 

The story of **Johannesburg** is irrevocably tied to what lies beneath its soil. Founded in 1886 following the discovery of gold, the city grew almost overnight from a humble mining camp into a booming industrial hub. This rapid rise drew people from all corners of the globe, establishing a diverse, multi-ethnic tapestry that continues to define the city today.

However, **Johannesburg** is far more than just a site of commerce; it is the historic epicenter of **South Africa’s** long struggle for freedom and democracy. Key sites throughout the city offer a sobering yet inspiring look into the past. In Soweto, a sprawling township southwest of the city center, visitors can walk down Vilakazi Street—the only street in the world to have been home to two Nobel Peace Prize laureates, Nelson Mandela and Archbishop Desmond Tutu. Nearby, the world-renowned Apartheid Museum and Constitution Hill stand as monumental reminders of the country's journey from oppression to reconciliation.

In the modern era, **Johannesburg** has undergone a thrilling urban renaissance. It has transformed into a global hub for contemporary African art, fashion, and music. Districts like the Maboneng Precinct and Braamfontein are alive with colorful murals, indie galleries, rooftop bars, and vibrant weekend markets. It is also the birthplace of groundbreaking musical movements, from the historical rhythms of Kwaito to the modern, globally dominating beats of Amapiano.

Contrasting its rich cultural scene is the sleek skyline of Sandton, often called "Africa's richest square mile," which serves as the financial epicenter of the region. Yet, despite its concrete skyscrapers and fast-paced lifestyle, **Johannesburg** holds a surprising secret: it is widely recognized as one of the largest man-made urban forests in the world, boasting over six million trees that carpet the suburban landscape in brilliant green.

**Johannesburg** is a city of striking contrasts—where history and the future collide, and where grit meets glamour. It does not possess the coastal calm of Cape Town, but it offers something entirely unique: a raw, authentic glimpse into the soul, resilience, and boundless optimism of modern **South Africa**.

**CAPE TOWN, South Africa (CNN)** — A deadly wave of anti-immigrant violence that has paralyzed parts of Johannesburg for nearly two weeks has officially spread to South Africa’s coastal tourism hub, with xenophobic mobs attacking foreign nationals in the informal settlements surrounding Cape Town.

Tear gas and rubber bullets echoed through the township of Du Noon, north of Cape Town, on Friday as police struggled to disperse crowds of armed locals hunting down foreign residents. Burnt-out shells of foreign-owned shops littered the streets, while thousands of desperate immigrants sought shelter at local police stations, churches, and community halls.

The violence, which erupted on May 11 in the Alexandra township of Johannesburg, has now escalated into a national crisis, claiming at least 42 lives, displacing an estimated 20,000 people, and casting a grim shadow over the country’s post-apartheid identity.

"We thought Cape Town would be safe," said Joseph Moyo, a 34-year-old Zimbabwean tailor who fled his home in the Khayelitsha township overnight after a mob smashed his windows. "They came with sticks and pangas [machetes], yelling that foreigners must go. We ran with nothing. Now we are sleeping on the concrete outside the police station."

### A crisis migrating south

For over ten days, authorities insisted the violence was contained to Gauteng province, the economic heartland surrounding Johannesburg and Pretoria. But over the week, flames of resentment traveled hundreds of miles south and east, striking KwaZulu-Natal and the Eastern Cape before igniting in the Western Cape.

By Thursday night, the violence had firmly reached Cape Town's vast, impoverished "Cape Flats"—sprawling townships where millions of poor South Africans live alongside immigrants from Zimbabwe, Mozambique, Somalia, Malawi, and the Democratic Republic of Congo.

In Masiphumelele, a township near the tourist-heavy area of Noordhoek, foreign shopkeepers were systematically targeted. Eyewitnesses reported seeing groups of young men roaming streets, pulling foreigners from their homes, and looting small grocery stores, known locally as "spaza" shops.

"It is a shame upon our nation," said Western Cape Premier Ebrahim Rasool during an emergency press briefing in Cape Town. "What we are seeing is a virus of hatred spreading across our country, and we must meet it with the full force of the law."

### Government struggles to respond

The rapid spread of the violence has put immense pressure on the administration of President Thabo Mbeki, which has faced fierce criticism for being too slow to act. 

In an unprecedented move earlier this week, Mbeki approved the deployment of the South African National Defence Force (SANDF) to assist overwhelmed police officers in Gauteng—marking the first time the military has been deployed domestically to quell violence since the end of white-minority rule in 1994. 

Local officials in Cape Town have requested similar military intervention as safe havens in the city rapidly reach capacity. Over 5,000 displaced foreigners are currently camped out at various collection points across the Cape Peninsula, with local aid organizations warning of an impending humanitarian emergency.

"People need food, blankets, and sanitation immediately," said Helen Zille, Mayor of Cape Town. "We are working around the clock, but the sheer volume of displaced people arriving at police stations is overwhelming."

### Poverty and scapegoating

The root causes of the outbreak are complex, fueled by deep-seated economic frustration. Fourteen years after the fall of apartheid, millions of poor Black South Africans remain trapped in severe poverty, facing sky-high unemployment rates, a severe housing shortage, and rising food prices.

Foreign immigrants—an estimated three million of whom have fled political violence and economic collapse in neighboring Zimbabwe—have become easy targets for localized anger. Local residents frequently accuse foreign nationals of stealing jobs, undercutting wages, driving up local crime, and taking spot allocations for subsidized government housing.

Human rights organizations have condemned the attacks and urged the South African government to address underlying xenophobia within local communities.

"This is not just criminal opportunistic behavior; it is driven by a dangerous narrative that blames the most vulnerable for systemic socio-economic failures," said a spokesperson for Amnesty International.

### Shadows over the future

The images of burning homes, heavily armed police, and frightened refugees contrast sharply with South Africa’s self-proclaimed status as the "Rainbow Nation." 

With the country set to host the FIFA World Cup in 2010, the violence has raised serious concerns internationally about safety and stability in Africa’s largest economy.

Back on the cold, wind-swept grounds of the Milnerton police station near Cape Town, families huddle under thin blankets as the sun sets over Table Mountain.

"We fled violence in our own countries to come here for peace," said Amina Said, a Somali mother of three, rocking her feverish toddler. "Now, there is nowhere left to run."

**BREAKING NEWS**

### SOUTH AFRICA DEPLOYS ARMY AS ANTI-FOREIGNER VIOLENCE SPREADS; DEATH TOLL RISES TO 42

**DATELINE:** JOHANNESBURG, South Africa – May 22, 2008  
**Byline:** Global News Desk

South Africa’s government has taken the unprecedented step of calling in the military to quell a wave of brutal xenophobic violence that has swept across the nation’s economic heartland, leaving at least 42 people dead, hundreds injured, and tens of thousands of African immigrants displaced. 

In an emergency announcement, President Thabo Mbeki approved a request from the South African Police Service (SAPS) for the South African National Defence Force (SANDF) to deploy troops to affected townships in Gauteng province. This marks the first time since the end of apartheid in 1994 that the South African military has been mobilized internally to contain domestic civil unrest.

For nearly two weeks, mobs of armed youths in townships surrounding Johannesburg and Pretoria have targeted foreign nationals—primarily immigrants from neighboring Mozambique, Zimbabwe, Malawi, and Somalia. Armed with pangas, axes, and petrol bombs, rioters have dragged foreigners from their homes, looted foreign-owned businesses, and set fire to informal settlements.

---

### MOUNTING DEATH TOLL AND HORRIFIC VIOLENCE

Police officials confirmed this morning that the official death toll has reached 42, though humanitarian groups warn the true figure is likely much higher as police continue to search charred shacks in informal settlements such as Ramaphosa, east of Johannesburg. 

In some of the most gruesome incidents captured by news cameras, victims have been beaten to death or burned alive. In Reiger Park, a Mozambican national was burned alive in front of a crowd as bystanders cheered, an image that has sent shockwaves across the globe and severely battered South Africa’s image as the "Rainbow Nation."

Gauteng Police Spokesperson Superintendent Billy Jones briefed reporters outside a heavily guarded police station in Johannesburg, confirming widespread arrests and the expansion of security operations.

"The situation in several areas remains extremely volatile, but security forces are moving in to restore order," Superintendent Billy Jones said. "We have arrested more than 400 suspects across the province on charges ranging from murder, attempted murder, and public violence to malicious damage to property and theft."

Jones urged calm and warned vigilantes that the police and army would show zero tolerance. "We are appealing to members of the public not to take the law into their own hands. Police, supported by the army, will remain on high alert and will act decisively against anyone found committing criminal acts, regardless of their grievances," Jones added.

---

### HUMANITARIAN CRISIS: MASS DISPLACEMENT OF ZIMBABWEANS AND MOZAMBICANS

The violence has triggered a massive humanitarian crisis, driving an estimated 30,000 to 50,000 foreign nationals from their homes. Police stations, community halls, and churches have been transformed into makeshift refugee camps, overwhelmed by thousands of frightened families seeking protection.

The crisis has hit immigrants from Zimbabwe and Mozambique particularly hard:

*   **Zimbabwean Refugees:** Millions of Zimbabweans have fled across the border into South Africa in recent years to escape hyperinflation, political violence, and economic collapse under President Robert Mugabe. Now, many find themselves trapped between persecution at home and terror in South Africa. At the Central Methodist Church in downtown Johannesburg, over 1,500 Zimbabweans are sleeping in hallways and stairwells, terrified to step outside.
*   **Mozambican Exodus:** Thousands of Mozambicans are abandoning their possessions and fleeing back across the border. The Mozambican government has set up emergency transit camps near the Ressano Garcia border post to process thousands of traumatized citizens returning on overloaded buses and trucks. Maputo has declared a temporary state of emergency to manage the influx.

"We fled Mugabe to come here to survive, but now they are hunting us like animals," said Tendai Moyo, a 29-year-old Zimbabwean teacher currently sheltering at a police station in Alexandra township. "We have nowhere left to run."

---

### UNDERLYING ECONOMIC FRUSTRATIONS AND SCAPEGOATING

While political leaders, including President Mbeki, have condemned the violence as pure criminality, sociologists and economists point to deep-seated socioeconomic grievances plaguing South Africa’s impoverished townships.

Fourteen years after the fall of apartheid, millions of black South Africans remain trapped in severe poverty. The violence has erupted against a backdrop of deteriorating economic conditions, including:

1.  **Staggering Unemployment:** Official unemployment in South Africa hovers around 23%, but in informal settlements, youth unemployment exceeds 50%.
2.  **Housing and Resource Shortages:** A critical shortage of government-subsidized (RDP) housing has led to long waiting lists, breeding resentment toward immigrants who are perceived as jump-starting the queue or illegally renting shacks.
3.  **Rising Cost of Living:** A global surge in food and fuel prices in early 2008 has hit South Africa’s poorest citizens hardest, pushing households to the brink of survival.

Local vigilantes have scapegoated foreign nationals, accusing them of stealing jobs by accepting below-minimum wages, undercutting local spaza shop owners, driving up crime rates, and strain basic public services like healthcare and sanitation.

"The competition for basic survival in the townships is fierce," said Dr. Loren Landau, Director of the Forced Migration Studies Programme at the University of the Witwatersrand. "What we are seeing is not just random criminality, but the violent manifestation of broken promises. Poorer South Africans feel abandoned by the state, and foreign migrants have become the easiest targets for their rage."

---

### GLOBAL CONDEMNATION AND SPREADING FEARS

The violence threatens to spread beyond Gauteng. Sporadic reports of anti-foreigner intimidation and clashes have emerged from the Western Cape and KwaZulu-Natal, prompting fear that the violence could paralyze the entire nation.

The African Union (AU), the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), and international human rights organizations have strongly condemned the attacks, urging the South African government to protect vulnerable migrant populations. 

As military convoys begin rolling into the affected townships tonight, South Africa faces its gravest moral and security challenge since the dawn of its democracy—forced to confront the harsh reality that the dream of a united, pan-African "Rainbow Nation" is fracturing under the weight of poverty and xenophobia.

### ECHOES OF A DARK PAST: Xenophobic Attacks Unleash Terror in South Africa, Sparking Regional Crisis and Evacuations

**By David Khumalo and Elena Santos**

**JOHANNESBURG —** The fragile image of South Africa as the "Rainbow Nation" lies shattered this week under a pall of thick black smoke. What began ten days ago as localized anti-immigrant skirmishes in the impoverished township of Alexandra has erupted into a full-scale regional crisis, characterized by horrific mob violence, displacement, and the terrifying resurgence of apartheid-era execution methods.

At least 42 people have been killed, hundreds injured, and more than 30,000 foreign nationals displaced as armed mobs roam the informal settlements of Gauteng, the East Rand, and Durban. Armed with pangas, sjamboks, and makeshift torches, South African assailants have dragged immigrants from their homes, accusing them of stealing jobs, driving up crime, and hoarding government housing.

#### The Return of the Tire: Apartheid Tactics Revived

What has shocked human rights observers and political leaders alike is not merely the scale of the xenophobia, but the sickening brutality of the tactics being deployed—tactics once used by anti-apartheid activists against police informants in the 1980s. 

In the Ramaphosa informal settlement near Reiger Park earlier this week, photojournalists captured horrifying images of a foreign man—believed to be a Mozambican national—burned alive after a crowd forced a petrol-doused tire over his torso. The victim, whose agonizing death has sparked outrage worldwide, fell prey to "necklacing," a gruesome signature of South Africa’s violent political past.

"To see the necklace method return, not against the oppressors of the past, but against fellow Africans who harbored us during the struggle, is a moral failure beyond words," said a distraught community activist in Johannesburg, who requested anonymity out of fear for his safety. "We fought for liberation only to turn into the monsters we once fought against."

#### Mozambique Braces for Fallout as Thousands Flee

The brutality has triggered an immediate and furious reaction across Southern Africa, nowhere more severely than in neighboring Mozambique. Mozambicans, alongside Zimbabweans, have borne the brunt of the attacks. 

In Maputo, the Mozambican government has declared a state of emergency to handle the sudden influx of thousands of traumatized citizens fleeing South Africa. Transport hubs in Johannesburg are overwhelmed with Mozambicans attempting to board packed buses and trucks, leaving behind livelihoods built over decades.

At the Ressano Garcia border post, relief workers are struggling to manage humanitarian camps set up to accommodate the thousands of refugees streaming across the frontier every 24 hours. Many arrive with nothing more than the clothes on their backs, having seen their shops looted and homes torched.

In Maputo, public outrage is turning into diplomatic strain. The Mozambican Cabinet held an urgent session on Wednesday, with Prime Minister Luisa Diogo calling the events "deeply distressing and unacceptable." 

Tensions have already spilled over into the economic sector. Near the southern Mozambican town of Inhambane, Mozambican workers at a major natural gas project managed by the South African energy giant Sasol staged wildcat strikes and protests. South African employees on the site had to be briefly evacuated due to fears of retaliatory violence.

"If South Africa does not want us, they must tell us," said Jose Cossa, a Mozambican miner who fled his home in Primrose, Germiston. "My grandfather worked in the South African mines. We helped build their economy during apartheid. Now they burn us like dogs."

#### A Government Struggling to Respond

Critics have blasted President Thabo Mbeki’s administration for a sluggish and flat-footed response. For days, government officials dismissed the attacks as the work of "ordinary criminals" rather than acknowledging the systemic xenophobia fueling the crisis. 

It was only yesterday, after days of mounting casualties and international condemnation, that President Mbeki authorized the deployment of the South African National Defence Force (SANDF) to assist the police—the first time army troops have been deployed to quell domestic unrest in South Africa since the end of white-minority rule in 1994.

For Southern Africa, the psychological scars of May 2008 will take years to heal. **JOHANNESBURG, South Africa (CNN)** -- Smoke hung thick over the Alexandra township on Monday as heavily armed police fired rubber bullets and tear gas to disperse mobs hunting foreign nationals, in an escalating wave of xenophobic violence that is rapidly spreading across South Africa's major urban centers.

What began a week ago as localized skirmishes in the impoverished settlements northeast of Johannesburg has erupted into a nationwide humanitarian emergency. Mobs armed with pangas, iron bars, and petrol bombs have swept through informal settlements, dragging immigrants from their homes, looting foreign-owned shops, and setting shacks ablaze.

According to South African Police Service officials, at least 22 people have been killed, hundreds injured, and more than 13,000 driven from their homes over the past seven days. 

"They came in the middle of the night shouting that foreigners must go back home," said Tendai Mukasa, 34, a Zimbabwean construction worker currently taking shelter outside a police station in downtown Johannesburg along with hundreds of frightened women and children. "I fled Robert Mugabe's police in Harare last year to survive. Now, my neighbors here burned everything I own. I have nowhere left to run."

### Spreading to New Fronts

By late Monday, violence had spilled out of Johannesburg’s traditional flashpoints—such as Hillbrow, Cleveland, and Primrose—and reached the outskirts of Pretoria, the nation's administrative capital. Reports of intimidation and arson were also emerging from the coastal hub of Durban, sparking fears that the unrest could engulf the entire country.

Churches, community centers, and police station parking lots have been transformed into makeshift refugee camps. Humanitarian agencies, including the Red Cross, warned that basic supplies of food, blankets, and sanitation are rapidly running out.

"This is a crisis of unprecedented proportions for post-apartheid South Africa," said Patrick Matlou, a human rights researcher in Johannesburg. "The police are visibly overwhelmed, and the state was completely unprepared for the speed at which this violence metastasized."

### Economic Despair and Scapegoating

Fourteen years after the end of white-minority rule, South Africa remains plagued by vast economic inequality. Official unemployment hovers near 23 percent, while millions live in informal settlements without electricity, running water, or adequate sanitation.

Community leaders say deep-seated frustrations over the government’s failure to deliver housing and jobs have been redirected toward African migrants, particularly those from Mozambique, Malawi, and neighboring Zimbabwe. Immigrants are frequently accused by local residents of driving down wages, monopolizing public health resources, and fueling violent crime.

"Our people are starving while the government gives houses to foreigners," said Sipho Dlamini, a 28-year-old unemployed resident in Reiger Park, standing near the charred remains of a Mozambican-owned grocery store. "We are not against our African brothers, but South Africans must come first."

### The Zimbabwean Influx

At the heart of the demographic strain is the catastrophic meltdown of neighboring Zimbabwe. Under the increasingly authoritarian rule of President Robert Mugabe, Zimbabwe's economy has completely collapsed, suffering from hyperinflation estimated by independent economists to be well over 100,000 percent. 

A contested presidential election in March 2008 between Mugabe and opposition leader Morgan Tsvangirai brought a fresh wave of state-sponsored political violence, driving tens of thousands of Zimbabweans across the Limpopo River into South Africa each month. Human rights groups estimate that up to 3 million Zimbabweans are currently living—mostly undocumented—in South Africa.

"South Africa has been absorbing the regional fallout of the Zimbabwean crisis for years," said Dr. Elizabeth Rankine, an analyst at the Southern African Migration Programme. "The government in Pretoria tried to ignore the refugee crisis on its doorstep, and now the pressure valve has blown."

### Government Under Fire

President Thabo Mbeki's administration is facing intense criticism both at home and abroad for its delayed response to the crisis. Mbeki, who has long championed a vision of an "African Renaissance" and maintained a policy of "quiet diplomacy" toward Mugabe's government, condemned the violence in a national address late Sunday, calling it an "absolute disgrace."

"To kill and attack fellow Africans simply because they come from outside our borders goes against everything our liberation struggle stood for," Mbeki said. 

However, opposition parties and civil society organizations are demanding that the government deploy the South African National Defence Force (SANDF) to support the police—a drastic measure not taken in domestic civilian areas since the end of apartheid.

As night fell over Johannesburg on Monday, the sounds of police sirens and distant gunfire echoed through the city’s southern suburbs. For thousands of refugees huddling under plastic sheets in police station yards, the dream of South Africa as a safe haven has crumbled.

"We thought South Africa was the land of freedom," said Mukasa, wrapping a thin blanket around his shivering 4-year-old daughter. "Now we see it is just another battleground."
